clue.text: Will Self regularly rebuffed commendations and words from well-wishers

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
to rebuff is to push back, so the kept letters are sent back the other way

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the novelist's name
citations are formal official commendations

explanation.surface: The novelist Will Self keeps turning down praise and kind messages from his admirers.
explanation.walkthrough: Will Self is a real British novelist, which makes the name read as a person; here it is only a string of letters to pick from.
explanation.definitionFit: Congratulatory messages sent by people wishing someone well are exactly what felicitations are; a direct synonym.

clue.text: A good way to attempt to hide a right flipping mess

indicators.note: what hides something keeps it inside, so one piece goes within another
flipping something over turns it round so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: a good way off is far away
A plus R, the abbreviation for right
to have a go is to attempt something

explanation.surface: Advice on trying to cover up a complete and utter mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British expletive qualifying 'mess', but it reverses only the short 'a right' piece before it is hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrago is a confused jumble or hotchpotch of things, so it is a synonym for a muddle or disorder.

clue.text: French city not very well encapsulated in an article there

indicators.note: something encapsulated is sealed inside a capsule, so it sits within the other piece

blocks.note: someone not very well is ill
le is a definite article in France, the 'there' of the clue

explanation.surface: A French city feeling poorly, wrapped up in a newspaper article written there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' points back to France, so the article is the French word LE rather than an English A or THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lille is a large city in northern France near the Belgian border, an example of the category named.

clue.text: About to wake up and drink

blocks.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
to arouse someone is to wake them up

explanation.surface: Someone about to wake up and reach for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of the phrase 'about to', but it stands alone as C.
explanation.definitionFit: To carouse is to drink plentifully and make merry, so the verb is a livelier synonym for boozing.

clue.text: What you may need to get through to another person?

definitions.text: What you may need to get through to another person?

blocks.note: surface reading: managing to make someone understand you, or reaching them emotionally

blocks.clueFragment: What you may need to get through
blocks.note: setter's reading: to get through is to be connected on a call, which needs the digits to dial

explanation.walkthrough: 'Get through to' suggests persuading or connecting emotionally, but on the phone it means a call being connected.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialling a person's digits connects your call, so the string of digits is what lets you reach them by phone.

clue.text: Not just any flash British gangsters

blocks.note: the definite article picks out a particular one rather than just any
a mo is a moment, as is a flash
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: Not just any flashy British gangsters, but particularly showy ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' reads as the adjective for showy, but it is the noun meaning an instant, giving MO.
explanation.definitionFit: The organised criminal underworld, especially the Mafia, is commonly called by this collective name.

clue.text: Old record is guarded by unreasonable audio specialist

indicators.note: something guarded has protectors placed around it on either side

blocks.note: OTT, over the top, means excessive or unreasonable
O is the abbreviation for old
a log is a written record
taken as written

explanation.surface: A vinyl collector's old disc is protected by an unreasonable sound engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Audio specialist' suggests a sound engineer, but it is a doctor of the ear. OTT is the British abbreviation for over the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Otology is the medical study of the ear, so its practitioner is an expert in hearing.

clue.text: We tucked into small serving of food like köttbullar?

indicators.note: to tuck into is to be pushed snugly inside something

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
taken as written
a dish is a serving of food

explanation.surface: Diners tucking into a small plate of meatballs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucked into' suggests eating, but it signals insertion. The question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Köttbullar are the meatballs of Sweden, so they are an example of that country's national cuisine.

clue.text: Some unpopular opinions about certain type of vaccine

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters are taken from within the words
turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the last three letters of the first word and the first of the second

explanation.surface: Anti-vaccine sentiment: unpopular views about one kind of jab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like it means 'concerning', but it reverses the run of letters LARO.
explanation.definitionFit: Some vaccines, like the polio drops, are swallowed rather than injected; the adjective describes that kind.

clue.text: Continued amassing money, or surrendered?

blocks.note: first meaning: a lottery jackpot that was not won carries forward and grows
second meaning: gave in without a fight, like a dog showing its belly

explanation.walkthrough: One sense is financial: an unclaimed jackpot or an investment carried forward. The other is the informal idea of submitting meekly.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb covers both a prize fund carried into the next draw and giving in tamely without resistance.

clue.text: Messily eat a Gü dessert, perhaps

indicators.note: doing something messily leaves things in disorder, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters as printed, with the accent ignored

explanation.surface: Someone eating a Gü pudding messily.
explanation.walkthrough: Gü is a British brand of chocolate puddings, so it sits naturally in the surface; the umlaut is dropped as usual.
explanation.definitionFit: A gateau is a rich layered cream cake, one example of a sweet course served after a meal.

clue.text: Picture of noodle soup meeting size guidelines?

blocks.note: pho is a Vietnamese noodle soup
made to fit is made to measure, meeting the required size

explanation.surface: A photo of a bowl of soup that conforms to portion-size rules.
explanation.walkthrough: A Photofit is the British police name for a composite face picture of a suspect built from witness descriptions.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an assembled image of a face, so it counts as a kind of likeness or portrait used by detectives.

clue.text: Drug squad member working on a lead?

definitions.text: Drug squad member working on a lead?

blocks.clueFragment: Drug squad member working on a lead?
blocks.note: surface reading: a narcotics detective following up a clue in an investigation
setter's reading: a sniffer animal walked on a leash by its handler

explanation.walkthrough: 'Working on a lead' sounds like pursuing a clue, but a lead is also a leash.
explanation.definitionFit: Sniffer animals trained to detect narcotics serve with drug units and are walked on a leash by handlers.

clue.text: Big lizard droppings collected by one academic

indicators.note: things collected are gathered up and held, so one piece is held inside the others

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
guano is bird or bat droppings
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A professor gathers up the droppings left by a large reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: A don is a fellow at Oxford or Cambridge; with the Roman one in front, the pair surround the droppings.
explanation.definitionFit: The iguanodon was a large plant-eating dinosaur, and its name means iguana tooth, so lizard is loosely fair.

clue.text: Fine and kinda sorta brill, maybe

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencils
ish is the informal suffix or word for 'more or less'

explanation.surface: Something that is fine and sort of brilliant, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brill' reads as British slang for brilliant, but it is a flatfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Brill is a European flatfish related to turbot, an example of the class of aquatic animal.

clue.text: Total prejudice ultimately knocked back some Aussie natives

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
knocked back means sent backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a sum is a total
its final letter

explanation.surface: Total prejudice in the end rebuffed some native Australians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aussie natives' suggests people, but these are birds native to Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Emus are large flightless birds found only in Australia, so they are indigenous creatures of that country.

clue.text: Otherworldly, oddball heretic

indicators.note: an oddball is eccentric and out of the ordinary, so the letters fall into an unusual order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An eccentric heretic with an unearthly air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddball' looks like an adjective describing the heretic, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Etheric relates to the ether, an airy celestial substance, so it describes something ethereal and not of this world.

clue.text: Intro to revised volume includes new translation

indicators.note: an intro is the opening, so only the first letter is kept
to include something is to take it in, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: its first letter
an edition is a printed volume of a book
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: The introduction to a revised book contains a fresh translation.
explanation.walkthrough: R comes first, then EDITION takes N inside after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendition can mean a rendering of a text into another language, so it is a synonym for a version or interpretation.

clue.text: Tip dirt on your smartest clothes? That’s extremely stupid

indicators.note: to tip something is to tilt it over, turning the letters the other way

blocks.note: mud is wet dirt
your best, or Sunday best, are your finest clothes

explanation.surface: Throwing dirt over your finest outfit would be the height of folly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' reads as dump, but it turns MUD over to DUM, which then goes on BEST.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of a slang word for stupid means the most foolish of all, matching the clue's intensifier.

clue.text: Oppressive individual, awake endlessly

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: one is a single individual
to rouse is to awake

explanation.surface: A tyrannical person who stays awake all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oppressive individual' looks like one noun phrase meaning a tyrant, but the definition is just the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Onerous means burdensome or heavy to bear, so it is a near synonym for oppressive duties or loads.

clue.text: Endeavour to cut tree over shrub

indicators.note: a piece that cuts another slices into its middle
turned over means upside down, so in a down entry the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to try is to endeavour
the elm is a tree

explanation.surface: An attempt to fell a tree that stands over a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: TRY cuts into ELM to make EL(TRY)M, and the whole is then turned over.
explanation.definitionFit: Myrtle is an evergreen bush with fragrant white flowers, an example of the woody plant category.

clue.text: Playing Uno with Kathy? You shouldn’t have!

indicators.note: playing with things moves them about, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words joined, with 'with' as a link

explanation.surface: Kathy is handed a game of Uno as a gift and gushes in gratitude.
explanation.walkthrough: Uno is a card game, which makes 'Playing' look literal; here it shuffles the letters of the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: The polite exclamation on receiving a gift is a way of expressing gratitude, the same as the stock phrase.

clue.text: Type of festive wine drunk without hesitation

indicators.note: without means lacking, so something is removed

blocks.note: mullered is British slang for very drunk
er is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A seasonal wine knocked back quickly, without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like describing the wine being consumed, but it is slang for intoxicated; mullered is British slang for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulled wine is heated with spices and sugar, a classic Christmas drink, so the adjective names that kind.

clue.text: Unfamiliar jargon requires spelling out, partially

indicators.note: partially means only in part, so the letters come from within the words

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Technical terms you don't know need explaining, at least in part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spelling out' reads as explaining, but the letters lie across its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is informal for specialist vocabulary or a foreign tongue that an outsider finds strange.

clue.text: Trustworthy form of ID bracelet

indicators.note: a new form of something is a reshaping, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An identity bracelet as a reliable form of identification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form of ID' reads as a phrase about identification documents, but 'form of' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Creditable can mean deserving belief or credit, so in older usage it is a synonym for reliable or believable.

clue.text: Corner is not to be cut, you understand?

indicators.note: something cut is shortened, so a letter is lopped off the end

blocks.note: taken as written
OK? asks for confirmation that you have understood

explanation.surface: A firm instruction that corners must not be cut, and a check you understand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not to be cut' reads as a ban, but it tells you to clip the T from NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a small recess or sheltered angle in a room, so it is a synonym for a corner.

clue.text: Making bishops possibly snort cocaine’s absurd!

indicators.note: something absurd makes no sense, so the letters are in a nonsensical order

blocks.note: the letters as printed, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: The idea of bishops taking drugs is ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making bishops' reads as forcing clerics to do something, but it is the definition: the ceremonies that create them.
explanation.definitionFit: A consecration is the formal ceremony ordaining a cleric to a sacred office, such as elevating a priest to the episcopate.
